newsitem.title: GERMANY: Ex-Mercedes head sad to leave "best job in world".
newsitem.headline: Ex-Mercedes head sad to leave "best job in world".

text.p: Helmut Werner, who quit as head of Mercedes-Benz AG last week, said he had decided to give up "the best job in the world" to avoid permanent friction with Juergen Schrempp, chief of parent Daimler-Benz AG.

In his first interview since stepping down in an apparent power struggle over Schrempp's plan to merge Mercedes into the Daimler company, Werner said their differences were not personal and that they would still be meeting for drinks in 10 years.
But he said he saw no useful role for himself in the revamped group.
"It was gloomy day," Werner told Der Spiegel magazine.
The reorganisation at Germany's largest industrial group did not meet two preconditions he had set himself for staying.
"Firstly I had to be able to create added value for the company, and secondly there had to be no permanent area of preprogrammed friction with chief executive Schrempp."
Spiegel released the interview ahead of publication in Monday's editions.
Car and truck maker Mercedes accounts for 70 percent of Daimler's sales and nearly all its profits and Werner strongly believed his company should remain fully independent.

"One must be able to separate the hard dispute over the issues from personal relations. Mr Schrempp told me at my sixtieth birthday he wants to still be sharing a bottle of red wine with me in 10 years. I know we will be able to do that."

Recently voted by Business Week magazine as among the top 25 managers in the world -- the only German in the group -- Werner took Mercedes from an 800 million mark loss to a net profit of 2.3 billion marks after becoming chief executive in 1993.
But analysts have praised Schrempp's plan for creating a leaner, more profitable company because it will slash layers of middle and upper management, speeding up decision making.

Under the restructuring, to be formally approved at a supervisory board meeting on January 23, Mercedes will be represented on the Daimler board by three executives, one for cars, one for trucks and one for marketing.
Werner said the revamp preserved the "unity of management" he had demanded. The changes leave Daimler-Benz Aerospace AG (DASA) and Debis AG as separate subsidiaries.
Werner said Mercedes had turned itself into the most profitable carmaker in Europe in 1995. "And we again increased our profit last year."
"The enormous progress in rationalising means we can offer new models at very attractive prices. Last year we for the first time sold more than 640,000 cars."
The company had also entered new markets with the smaller two-seat A-class, an offroad vehicle and the Smart car.
He described speculation that he would take over as head of Volkswagen AG or the German railway as "very irritating and unnecessary."
Asked why he waited until now to resign when the basic plan for the revamp had been in place before Christmas, Werner said he had wanted to stay on to make final improvements.
"But admittedly -- if you have the best job in the world such a step is of course difficult to take."
Werner denied a newspaper report that he would receive an eight million-mark payoff.
He said he had not yet thought about what job to do next. "But one thing is sure: there will not yet be a pensioner Helmut Werner who only plays tennis and goes skiing."
